easy.explanation: Psalm 79:1 says, “the heathen are come into thine inheritance.”
easy.q: Who came into the LORD’s inheritance?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “thy holy temple have they defiled.”
The KJV says, “they have laid Jerusalem on heaps.”
easy.q: How is Jerusalem described after the destruction?

medium.explanation: To lay a city on heaps means to reduce it to ruins.
medium.q: What does the phrase “laid Jerusalem on heaps” describe?

answers: They were given as food to birds and beasts
medium.explanation: Their bodies were given “to be meat unto the fowls of the heaven” and the beasts of the earth.
medium.q: What was done with the bodies of God’s servants and saints?

medium.explanation: The passage describes the temple being defiled, people being killed, and Israel becoming a reproach.
medium.q: Which sequence correctly follows the events in these verses?

answers: That the destruction included dishonor and humiliation
challenge.explanation: The lack of burial highlights the depth of the disaster and the humiliation suffered by the dead.
challenge.q: What does the statement “there was none to bury them” emphasize?

challenge.explanation: The neighbors are the peoples living around Israel who witnessed and mocked its suffering.
challenge.q: Who are “our neighbours” in this passage?

answers: A holy temple versus its defilement
challenge.explanation: The passage contrasts the holiness of the temple with its defilement and destruction.
challenge.q: What central contrast appears in these verses?

paragraphs.title: A Plea to Turn the Anger toward the Enemies

answers: How long the LORD’s anger will last
easy.explanation: He asks, “How long, LORD? wilt thou be angry for ever?”
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask at the beginning of this section?

easy.explanation: He asks God to pour out His wrath upon the heathen.
easy.q: Upon whom does the psalmist ask God to pour out His wrath?

answers: They devoured Jacob and laid waste his dwelling place
easy.explanation: Psalm 79:7 says, “they have devoured Jacob, and laid waste his dwelling place.”
easy.q: What did the heathen do to Jacob and his dwelling place?

answers: They did not know God and had devastated Jacob
medium.explanation: They are described as nations that had not known God and had devoured Jacob.
medium.q: Why does the psalmist ask that God’s wrath be directed toward the heathen?

answers: That it is intense and consuming
medium.explanation: The comparison to fire expresses the intensity of God’s jealousy and anger.
medium.q: What does “burn like fire” communicate about God’s jealousy?

answers: The question about God’s anger leads to a request that it be directed at the enemies
The request cancels the description of the destruction
medium.explanation: After asking how long God’s anger will continue, the psalmist asks that it fall upon the nations that harmed Israel.
medium.q: How do verses 5–7 relate to one another?

answers: They know the LORD very well
They do not call upon or acknowledge the LORD
challenge.explanation: The phrase portrays them as people who have not called upon God’s name.
challenge.q: What does “that have not called upon thy name” reveal about the heathen?

answers: Because they devoured Jacob, they laid waste his dwelling place
Because they prayed, they were delivered
Because they gave thanks, the temple was rebuilt
challenge.explanation: The verse connects the enemies’ devouring of Jacob with the desolation of his dwelling place.
challenge.q: What cause and result are connected in verse 7?

answers: Those who harmed Israel deserve a response
The enemies’ actions have no significance
challenge.explanation: The psalmist asks God to direct His wrath toward the nations responsible for Israel’s devastation.
challenge.q: What view of justice does the psalmist express?

paragraphs.title: A Plea for Mercy, Deliverance, and the Honor of God’s Name

easy.explanation: They pray, “O remember not against us former iniquities.”
easy.q: What does the people ask God not to remember?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “for we are brought very low.”
easy.q: Why do they ask God to help them?

easy.explanation: He asks, “let him be known among the heathen” through the avenging of the blood of God’s servants.
easy.q: Among whom does the psalmist ask God to be known by the revenging of the blood?

answers: The building of a new city only
medium.explanation: The people ask for mercy, help, the purging of their sins, and deliverance for God’s name’s sake.
medium.q: What are the main requests in verses 8–9?

answers: We have become weak and helpless
medium.explanation: The phrase describes a condition of great weakness and distress.
medium.q: What does “we are brought very low” mean?

answers: For the glory and sake of His name
medium.explanation: They ask God to deliver them and purge away their sins “for thy name’s sake.”
medium.q: Why do the people ask God to purge away their sins?

answers: Deliverance would display the glory and power of God’s name
Deliverance was intended only for the birds
challenge.explanation: The people ask for help “for the glory of thy name” and for God to be known among the heathen.
challenge.q: What connection does the passage make between Israel’s deliverance and God’s glory?

answers: People destined or appointed to face death
challenge.explanation: The phrase refers to prisoners and others who are under sentence of death or in deadly danger.
challenge.q: Who are “those that are appointed to die”?

answers: From weakness and a plea for mercy to an open request for deliverance
challenge.explanation: The people confess their low condition, ask for mercy, and then plead for visible help and preservation.
challenge.q: What emotional movement occurs in verses 8–11?

paragraphs.title: Retribution for the Enemy and a Commitment to Praise

easy.explanation: He asks God to render unto the neighbors their reproach against the LORD.
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask God to render unto the neighbors?

answers: As God’s people and the sheep of His pasture
easy.explanation: The people say, “we thy people and sheep of thy pasture.”
easy.q: How is Israel described at the end of the psalm?

answers: Give thanks and show forth God’s praise
easy.explanation: They promise, “we will give thee thanks for ever” and show forth His praise.
easy.q: What does the people promise to do?

medium.explanation: “Sevenfold” expresses a full and greatly increased repayment.
medium.q: What does “sevenfold” communicate in the request concerning the neighbors?

answers: The reproach was directed against the LORD
The neighbors gave thanks to God
medium.explanation: The neighbors had reproached the LORD, as stated in verse 12.
medium.q: Why does the psalmist ask for repayment of the reproach?

answers: Because the people belong to God, they promise loyalty and praise
The people want to leave God
medium.explanation: The image expresses Israel’s belonging to God, followed by a promise of continual thanksgiving.
medium.q: What is the connection between calling Israel “sheep of thy pasture” and promising thanksgiving?

answers: It is intended to continue through succeeding generations
It will be given only once
It belongs only to the neighbors
challenge.explanation: The phrase indicates that God’s praise will be proclaimed from generation to generation.
challenge.q: What does “to all generations” show about the people’s praise?

answers: A request for repayment to the enemies versus Israel’s pledge of loyalty and praise
A description of building versus trading
A request for silence versus forgetting
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from asking for judgment on the reproaching neighbors to promising praise from God’s people.
challenge.q: What contrast appears between verses 12 and 13?

answers: The people’s identity and belonging to God
The psalmist’s separation from the people
challenge.explanation: The wording identifies Israel as God’s own people and the sheep of His pasture.
challenge.q: What does the shift to “we thy people” emphasize?
